messages.body_plain:
So, any number of methods for working with 'unmarked' animals often make the explicit assumption that an 'encountered' individual is not 'counted' >1 times (what one of my colleagues calls the 'classical conceit of the hot-shot field biologist who would never do that' - said colleague being more cynical than me).

Since distance sampling often falls under the larger umbrella of 'analysis of data from unmarked individiauls', was wondering if someone would point me at the canonical reference(s) for the analysis of the impact of the violation of this assumption on interesting things -- like (say) abundance (where even a naive assessment would suggest that >1 counts for some fraction of individuals would lead to a positive bias in N. I'm particular interested in how distance sampling congensceti would 'test' for a violation of this assumption (as opposed to the distance sampling diletante who might simply assume it never happens).

Cheers...

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] naive question
messages.body_plain:
Hi Evan,

The truth is that even a distance sampling diletante ;) - hey... I wonder if that is what I should add to my CV now... - does not need assume it never happens, it can happen and cause no problem whatsoever. You must need common sense to evaluate if it is a problem or not in a given scenario.

Imagine the situation where you cover the same transects 10 times, one time in each of 10 days. If you pool the data in the right way, you can still estimate an average density over the 10 days. You might actually have seen more animals than the number of animals you estimate to be there. But there's no problem about it. The point estimate and the corresponding variance of density can be obtained.

Random movement across lines will not matter either. For any animal you spot again in the next transect because the animal happened moved that way will on average be cancelled by an animal that was in transect 2 when you were going over transect 1 and moved to transect 1 when you were covering transect 2.

The real problem will occur if you drive animals from one transect to the next and them keep counting the same animal over and over again. Or if say you are surveying an area over which animals are migrating and the migration is not independent of the transect placement, say.

Does that help?

cheers

Tiago

Evan

To amplify what Tiago has said, the distance sampling assumption at issue in your question is "objects are detected at their initial location", hence about animal movement rather than about double counting.

The first paragraph of Section 2.1.2 of Buckland et al. (2001) would be a first port of call.  As to a "test" of animal movement, Figure 2.2 of same reference provides a qualitative measure of responsive movement (not double counting).

Distance sampling methods that incorporate the effect of movement are under development, beginning with an assessment of bias induced by movement developed by Glennie et al. (2015) PLoS ONE https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0121333

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] naive question
messages.body_plain:
Following up on Tiago’s comments, you can think of distance sampling as being a form of plot sampling where we estimate the proportion of animals detected on the plot.  So the effective size of the plot is this proportion multiplied by the actual size.  There is no reason why the effective sizes of the plots, when all added together, can’t exceed the size of the study area.  When that occurs, of course your sample size exceeds the population size.  There is a violation of the independence assumption, but given good survey design, coupled with variance estimation methods that are robust to failures of this assumption, the implications are mild.  In my 2006 Auk paper, I showed by simulation that for a point transect survey in which each bird is expected to be detected from on average between 3 and 4 points, bias was just one half of one percent, even though the number of detections far exceeded the population size.

Steve Buckland

> Ana
>
> You cover lots of topics in this email; hard to know where to begin.
>
> It is unfortunate your data are spiked and doubly unfortunate that this was not diagnosed until the end of the three years of data collection.  Nevertheless, the purpose of binning is to get the detection into the correct "bin" if it was not in the correct "exact" distance because of rounding.  To get data into the correct bin, it seems the "preferred" distance (multiple of 5) should be in the centre of the bin, not at the edge; so I would use cutpoints different to the ones you have used.  I might also believe (but you know better because the data are yours) that rounding was less of a problem at small distances than at large distances--suggesting that you have narrower bins at small distances--there is no reason that the bins need to be of the same width: perhaps 0-1, 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-6,...
>
> Because you have binned the data, you do not have the Kolomogorov-Smirnov or Cramer von-Mises tests at your disposal and you must use the chi-square test (which is sensitive to the location of the cutpoints for binning).  The degrees of freedom of the chi-square test is u-q-1 where u is the number of bins (6 in the example you provide) and q is the number of parameters in your model.  If you fit a hazard rate model with 2 parameters and include site as a factor covariate (adding 2 more parameters to be estimated), I think you will end up with 6-4-1=1 degrees of freedom left for your test.  Should an adjustment term appear in the fitted model you will see the "no degrees of freedom for test" message.
>
> If you are in this situation, then you are in the uncomfortable situation of making inference about thrush density based on a detection function model inconsistent with the data you observed.  You may say this lack of fit was caused by rounding of data in the field, but your inference will be somewhat tarnished.
>
> I believe to get year-specific estimates you would need to include Region.Label in your model; give that a try.

messages.body_plain:
Negative binomial and Poisson distributions are appropriate for modelling counts from distance sampling.  Probability of detection is addressed through an offset in the model.  That offset must be estimated.  But the model is still applied to integer counts.

Steve Buckland

Hi Kevin, hi listfolks,

Two quick things here:

1. you don't always need to use a Horvtiz-Thompson-ised response when
there are covariates in the detection function -- only when the
covariates vary at the scale of the observation. Transect-level
covariates like Beaufort sea state are fine to use count as the response
for. The way to think about it is: does the probability of detection
vary within segment? If it does, you need to use H-T (for now*), if
detectability only varies at the segment level, you can use count. I'm
working on a method of using count when detection covariates vary

2. I do recommend using the Tweedie in general as it can deal with the
various response types flexibly as it has continuous support.

Hope this helps.

--dave

* I'm working on a method of using count when detection covariates vary
within segment and will post something to the list once a preprint is ready.

Hi Steve, just to reopen this, I've been doing some reading, mostly from cetacean studies where detection on the transect line is often not 100% and varies based on weather conditions (Beaufort sea state in their cases). This seems like pretty much the exact same thing going on in my avian study, where even after correction via detection function, there are still large differences between survey counts on the basis of weather conditions, time of day, etc. Barlow (2015) appeared to tackle this issue simply by including Beafort sea state in his presence-absence model (he was trying to estimate relative g(0) for each Beaufort level) - is that approach valid for application to a count model? Or is there a need to partition the analysis such that the unaccounted for detection covariates only apply to the zeros in the data? Basically I'm asking if a two stage modelling approach with presence-absence followed by poisson or whatever is necessary, or if i can stick with my current negative binomial model.

My apologies for asking so many questions lately. I'm in the late stages of my study, so i'm trying to make sure all the i's are dotted and t's are crossed analysis-wise.

Thanks again,
Kevin

In theory, if you’re still certain to detect them on the line or at the point, all should be OK, but if quiet birds move away from the observer, they may well escape detection.  Similarly, females are often undetected. In particular, start time of survey popped out as being highly significant in my dsm. Start time was not a significant covariate in my detection function modelling. Hi Kevin, List,

In case it's useful, we did something like this in a recent paper
modelling abundance of a small porpoise, the vaquita.
(https://doi.org/10.1111/conl.12331 -- technical details are in the
supplemental materials.)  There were a few differences: it was a
one-stage (Bayesian) model rather than two-stage; we modelled g0
affecting count rather than presence-absence; there were a few other
complications.

The danger in such models, where we put detectability variables into the
count or presence-absence model, is that if there is a correlation
between these variables and animal density then we have confounding
between detectability and density, and it is difficult to see how
density can be accurately inferred.  For example, if g0 is affected by
some habitat variable in your bird study such as vegetation type (birds
tend to sing in one type and not others, and you only detect birds
aurally), and so is density, then putting habitat type in as a covariate
will not allow you to accurately estimate density.  g0 must be inferred
some other way (e.g., by a double-observer method).  Hope this makes sense.

Cheers, Len

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Is there an easy way to obtain the prediction of the detection probability considering specific covariates values and a specific distance ?

The predict function can give me an average conditional detection probability over the whole range of distance considered (0 to W or int.range), but in my case, I want to know what this detection probability is, for example, at 40 m from the observer.

#######################################
To illustrate my question:

data(book.tee.data)
egdata <- book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe[book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe$observer==1,]
egdata$Covar1 <- sample(seq(1,16), nrow(egdata), replace=TRUE) # Create a fake covariate
head(egdata)

result <- ddf(dsmodel=~mcds(key="hn", formula=~1), data=egdata, method="ds", meta.data=list(width=4))
predict(result, newdata=egdata) # Because no covariates were included -> same value everywhere.

result <- ddf(dsmodel=~mcds(key="hn", formula=~Covar1), data=egdata, method="ds", meta.data=list(width=4))
predict(result, newdata=egdata) # average detection probability for each specific value of the covariate

newdat <-  egdata
newdat$distance <- runif(nrow(newdat),0.1,4)
predict(result, newdata=newdat) # (Obviously) same as previous even if distance was changed

## I need the specific detection probability corresponding to the distance defined for each line of the new dataset.

Thanks

Arnaud

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'd like to know what folks think of the attached randomized quantile residuals vs linear predictor plot. I thought rqgam.check() was supposed to randomize out the artifacts caused by the discrete nature of the data, but plainly in the plot, it appears as though only the zeros have gotten that treatment. This does not occur in negative binomial rq plots of the same data, so is this just because tweedie expects continuous data ergo qres.tweedie() doesn't apply the randomization, whereas negative binomial expects discrete? Or is this a sign tweedie does not fit the data? The tweedie rq plots for all of my species groups look like this (more or less). Despite the artifacts, it doesn't appear that there is much heterogeneity in the variance, so I'm thinking Tweedie isn't necessarily a bad fit.

I have a secondary question too. On occasion I am getting negative R.sq for negative binomial models, whereas the % deviance explained is perfectly reasonable (~30%). In tweedie models of the same data, all of a sudden this is not an issue and R.sq is a reasonable value close to %dev. Same data, same covariates, so it doesn't seem as though the models are overparameterized, which i know can be a cause of negative adjusted R.sq. The interesting thing is that nb() is preferable to tw() on the basis of AIC, so i'd use it, except that the negative R.sq is giving me pause. I would use tweedie, except for the aforementioned question about the rq plots.

Thanks for all your help,
Kevin

detfct(1, result$ds$aux$ddfobj)

*conditional on the observed covariates*. Supplying more than one
distance at the time gets a bit fraught as you fall victim to R's vector
recycling rules, which can get a bit tricky decipher when you have
covariates. I'd advise some caution when running such code for that reason.

Imene (list):

Thanks for the compliment Imene.

About your sample size question for density surface modelling (DSM).  This method used model-based inference to estimate the number of animals (or litter) in the portion of the study region not covered by your transects.  Because of this inferential procedure, it is not possible to provide a minimum number of transects.  Instead, formulate the question this way.  How much information must I acquire to have confidence in the model I construct as the basis for my model-based inference?

The answer to that question should include thought about the covariates you intend to use in your DSM model and the degree to which the statistical distribution in your sample mimics the statistical distribution of those covariates in the entire study area.  That is not a guaranteed way to prevent your model from producing invalid inference, but it is a start.  The paradox of this advice is its reliance upon your ability to know the statistical distribution of covariates across your entire study area.  Nevertheless, if these covariates are remotely sensed, you may be able to acquire reasonable knowledge about the statistical distribution of covariates you intend to employ.  You can then contrast the statistical distribution of covariates in your sample and decide if you need further survey effort for the distribution of covariates in your sample to better approximate the distribution of covariates in the study area.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sara

Your design sketch looks pretty good.  Answers to your specific questions:

a) yes, you can truncate distances in the field.  However, if you have transects 5m long, I would not truncate at 5m, because that will lead to large areas of overlap in coverage areas between legs of the zigzag. Simply sketch out a box that is 10m wide centred on each of your transect legs to see what I mean.  If you want your transects to be 5m in length, then perhaps your truncation distance might be only 2m.  Even then there will be overlap in coverage areas between consecutive legs.  You should create a decision rule about what to do with the overlap areas.  To which leg should those overlapping areas belong?

Have a look a the lecture describing this issue on our new online course:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter4/#design-of-distance-sampling-surveys (slides 12 and 13 of that lecture).

b) To create a random start, choose a random number between 0 and 100.  Start the first leg of your zigzag at that location along your "guiding medium line".  Lay your zigzag legs from there until you have your 20 legs, or until you run into the sea.  If you run into the sea before finishing your 20 legs, allocate the remaining legs starting at distance 0 (in this case you will have some of your legs near the sea and the remainder of legs near the beach top with a gap in effort in between).

c) The fitted detection function you sent suggests that detectability does not drop off very rapidly as a function of distance.  You appear to still be seeing ~80% of the objects out at your 5m truncation distance.  The overall proportion of objects you see within the truncation distance is ~90%.  There is nothing horrible about that.

I do wonder about the size of your pieces of litter relative to the scale of your measurements.  If the litter is bottles, they are small relative to the width of the cutpoints in the histogram.  However, if the litter is sheets of plastic or pieces of rope (often the type of beach litter we see here in Scotland), then it the rope can be >1m in length.  If so, what is the distance to the transect you are recording?  If you measure its closest distance, perhaps that is the explanation for the "spike" in the first distance bin.  I would suggest the better distance to record would be the average distance from the rope to the transect; more precisely the distance from the "centre" of the rope to the transect.  Have a look at this online lecture to see the concept described in context of groups of animals:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter4/#field-methods (slide 11)
